body:
# Independent audit of the uniform small-slope escape expansion

Audited source: `candidate c21aa22115d69526`.
Original finite-sum definition: Section 1 of
`candidate a38c69b78fd106d1`.

**Result: PASS.** The scaled kernels, quadrature identity, uniform
parameter control, moving-endpoint right integral, endpoint corrections,
and simultaneous a,v->0 limit are correct. The scalar input (S) is
supplied by `candidate 31c8bae81eb26cc3`;
this audit does not re-prove that independent theorem.

The argument concerns the precise diagonal-envelope deficit. It neither
compares the remaining double knots nor proves arbitrary mixed-integer OC.

## 1. Exact finite sums and scaling

Fix d>=2, t=1/(d+1), theta=d/(d+1), Gamma=theta^d. The original
deficit is

    D(a,beta)=Gamma sum_(h>=0)(1-ah)_+^d
       -sum_(h>=0)[E(t-beta h,(1-ah)_+)
                    +E(t+beta(h+1),(1-ah)_+)],
    E(q,r)=d^d q^(d-1)(r-dq)_+                         (r,q>0).

At zero-radius indices the envelope is defined to be zero. In the
parameter range 0<=beta<=at, every positive-radius threshold satisfies
q>=tr>0, so the formula never evaluates an inappropriate negative
threshold power.

Set v=beta/(at) and x=ah. Direct substitution and division by Gamma
give exactly

    L_v(x)=(1-vx)^(d-1)[1-(d+1-dv)x]_+,
    R_(a,v)(x)=(1+av+vx)^(d-1)
                         [1-dav-(d+1+dv)x]_+.

The first factors are nonnegative on each active interval. If
0<=a<=1/(2d), both supports are subsets of [0,1]; the right endpoint
is (1-dav)/(d+1+dv)>0. Outside their positive-part supports the
functions are defined to be zero. Thus these scaled sums retain
exactly the original finitely many fiber contributions, including
supporting knots and zero-radius endpoints.

## 2. Uniform quadrature, including derivative jumps

For a compactly supported continuous function g on [0,infinity)
whose right derivative has bounded variation, the identity is

    sum_(h>=0)g(ah)=(1/a) integral g+g(0)/2+E,
    |E|<=(a/8)Var(g').                                  (1)

On a grid interval [u,u+a], the exact trapezoid error is the integral
of (x-u)(u+a-x)/2 against the distributional derivative of g'.
That nonnegative kernel is at most a^2/8. Derivative jumps strictly
inside a grid interval are included by this Stieltjes integral.
A jump exactly at a grid endpoint has kernel value zero; one may
allocate such atoms to half-open intervals, so none is double-counted
when bounding by the global variation. Summing the finite collection
of nonzero interval errors and dividing by a proves (1). The left
endpoint value contributes g(0)/2 precisely as stated.

For the two scaled kernels, the active polynomial coefficients vary
over a compact parameter rectangle, their supports are uniformly
bounded, and the only possible jump in the first derivative is at
the final support endpoint. This proves uniform BV control. The
possible vanishing of the left first factor at v=1 creates no extra
jump or singular derivative. At d=2 its second-derivative term with
factor d-2 is absent, rather than an expression involving a negative
power at zero.

## 3. Right integral and its moving endpoint

Put A=1-dav, B=d+1+dv, C=1+av. On the relevant rectangle A>=1/2
and B>=d+1. The substitution x=(A/B)y gives

    I_R(a,v)=(A^2/B) sum_(j=0)^(d-1)
      binom(d-1,j) C^(d-1-j)(vA/B)^j/[(j+1)(j+2)].      (2)

Every factor and the integration weight y^j(1-y) checks directly.
This is a finite formula with bounded first and second a-derivatives
uniformly in v. Consequently

    I_R(a,v)=I_R(0,v)+aJ_d(v)+O_d(a^2)

is genuinely uniform, not an expansion at a fixed truncation index.
The function J_d is continuous and J_d(0)=0, because (2) has no
a-dependence when v=0.

The endpoint correction is also correct: L_v(0)=1 and
R_(a,v)(0)=(1+av)^(d-1)(1-dav)=1+O_d(a). Thus the two kernel
sums have constant term J_d(v)+1. The mass sum has constant term
1/2. Subtraction therefore gives -J_d(v)-1/2, not -J_d(v) or zero.
The right-fiber threshold's extra beta is retained as the av term
throughout this calculation.

## 4. Continuous integral and simultaneous limits

For v>0, write B_-=d+1-dv and A_-=(d+1)(1-v). The substitution
y=1-vx in the left integral gives

    I_L(v)=[B_-/(d+1)-A_-/d
               +A_-^(d+1)/(d(d+1)B_-^d)]/v^2.

The right integral at a=0 is obtained by replacing v with -v.
Adding gives exactly

    I_L(v)+I_R(0,v)=[f(v)+f(-v)-2]/(d v^2),
    f(v)=(1+v)^(d+1)/(1+theta v)^d.

At v=0 each integral is 1/[2(d+1)]. The continuous extension also
follows from the uniformly bounded supports and continuous original
integrands, without division by a small v in an error estimate.

Define G_d(v)=I_L(v)+I_R(0,v)-1/(d+1). The audited source therefore
has the exact uniform expansion

    D(a,atv)/Gamma=-G_d(v)/a-J_d(v)-1/2+O_d(a).          (3)

The scalar theorem makes G_d>=0 and strictly positive away from v=0.
For a sequence a->0, one may first choose a subsequence realizing
its limsup, then use compactness of [0,1] to make v converge. If its
limit is positive, the first term of (3) forces the deficit to minus
infinity. If v->0, drop that nonpositive term and use J_d(v)->0.
This proves the simultaneous, rate-free conclusion

    limsup_(a down to0, 0<=beta<=at) D(a,beta)<=-Gamma/2.

The explicit subsequence wording merely makes the usual limsup
argument fully transparent; it does not change the source's result.

## 5. An explicit cutoff, stronger than needed for attainment

The stronger scalar theorem supplies

    G_d(v)>=v^2/[4(d+1)].                                (4)

Here are fully explicit bounds on the other terms of (3). Define

    V_d=3d(3d+1)2^(d-3),
    T_d=2^(d-3)(9d^2-7d+2)/(d+1),
    E_d=(d+2)2^(d-4),
    C_d=V_d/4+d/8+T_d/2+E_d,
    K_d=[d(2d+1)/(d+1)^2]
                           [1+1/(d+1)]^(d-2).           (5)

For 0<=a<=1/(2d), 0<=v<=1, these constants give

    |J_d(v)|<=K_d v,
    |the remainder in (3)|<=C_d a.                      (6)

The following details verify every part of (6).

### 5.1. Variation of the scaled kernels

On its active interval either kernel has the form
g(x)=(C+sx)^(d-1)(A-Bx). The bounds

    0<=C+sx<=2, |s|<=1, 0<=A-Bx<=1, B<=2d+1

hold there, and the support length is at most one. Direct
differentiation gives

    |g'|<=(5d+1)2^(d-2),
    |g''|<=(d-1)(9d+2)2^(d-3).

At d=2 the term carrying d-2 is simply omitted. Adding the integral
bound for |g''| and the one possible final derivative jump proves
Var(g')<=V_d. Thus the two kernel quadrature errors together have
magnitude at most aV_d/4. The mass function (1-x)_+^d has derivative
variation exactly d, giving its error bound ad/8.

### 5.2. The right endpoint correction

The exact derivative of R_(a,v)(0) is

    partial_a R_(a,v)(0)
      =-v(1+av)^(d-2)(1+d^2av).

Since a<=1/(2d), its magnitude is at most
(d+2)2^(d-3). After multiplying by the endpoint weight 1/2,
the contribution to (3)'s remainder is at most aE_d.

### 5.3. Taylor remainder of the moving right integral

Let u(a)=A/B be the right support endpoint and Z=C+vx. Differentiating
under the integral once has no endpoint term, because the integrand
vanishes at u(a). On differentiating a second time, the boundary term
is IMPORTANT and equals

    [partial_a R(a,v,u(a))]u'(a)
       =d^2v^2 Z(u(a))^(d-1)/B.                         (7)

The interior second derivative is

    (d-1)(d-2)v^2 Z^(d-3)(A-Bx)
          -2d(d-1)v^2 Z^(d-2).

Using Z<=2, A-Bx<=1, B>=d+1, and the support length at most
1/(d+1), the integral of its absolute value plus the boundary term
(7) is at most T_d v^2<=T_d. Taylor's theorem gives a remainder
at most T_d a^2/2 in I_R, hence T_d a/2 in (3). Combining this with
Sections 5.1 and 5.2 proves the stated C_d bound.

### 5.4. A linear-in-v bound for J_d

At a=0 the first derivative has the explicit integral formula

    J_d(v)=-v integral_0^(1/B) (1+vx)^(d-2)
                     [1+(d^2-1+d^2v)x] dx,
    B=d+1+dv.

On this interval the power is at most [1+1/(d+1)]^(d-2),
the bracket is at most d(2d+1)/(d+1), and the interval length
is at most 1/(d+1). This proves |J_d(v)|<=K_d v, including v=0.

### 5.5. Completing the square

Equations (3), (4), and (6) imply

    D(a,atv)/Gamma
      <=-1/2-v^2/[4(d+1)a]+K_d v+C_d a
      <=-1/2+[C_d+(d+1)K_d^2]a.                         (8)

The last inequality is completion of the square and holds uniformly
for all v in [0,1]. In particular the explicit positive number

    epsilon_d=min{1/(2d),
                   1/[4(C_d+(d+1)K_d^2)]}              (9)

satisfies

    D(a,beta)<=-Gamma/4<0
       whenever 0<a<=epsilon_d and 0<=beta<=at.          (10)

This proves a concrete cutoff independently of any selected sequence
or maximizer. The constants are deliberately elementary bounds, not
claims of optimality.

## 6. Attainment consequence and remaining arithmetic problem

The source's exhibited pair a=2/(d+1), beta=1/[d(d+1)] gives positive
deficit Gamma sum_(h>=1)(1-2h/(d+1))_+^d for every d>=2.
Together with (10), the global maximum can be sought on the compact
domain epsilon_d<=a<=1, 0<=beta<=at. Its continuity there is exactly
the finite-sum continuity established in the double-knot note. Hence
the maximum is attained, and the already audited compact double-knot
reduction applies without a missing escape edge.

This audit does not compare the surviving integer pairs (H,J).
The location and sharp value of their maximum require a separate
proved arithmetic argument.
